name: SQL Injection Through AI
title: SQL Injection Through AI
answer: SQL injection is the insertion of malicious query text into a database command, and it has a newer cousin in systems where a language model writes the SQL. When an AI system generates SQL from user or document input, prompt injection can steer that generation toward harmful queries, so generated SQL needs the same controls as any untrusted input: least privilege, read only access where possible, and query review. The topic therefore sits at the meeting point of two older disciplines, database security and input handling, and one newer one, the behaviour of models that turn natural language into executable statements. The risk is not that the model is malicious but that it faithfully executes an instruction an attacker planted in text it was asked to read.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is familiar to anyone who has built a data application: a database engine, a driver or connector, an application layer, and now a model or agent that sits between the request and the query. The model may run as a hosted API call, a local model on the same host, or a component inside an orchestration framework that also holds credentials and connection strings. Because the generated query is executed by the same account the application uses, the database permissions attached to that account define the real blast radius. Logging, query history, and connection pooling all matter here, since they determine what can be reconstructed after a bad query runs. Retrieval layers that feed documents into the prompt are part of this picture too, because they are a common route for injected text to reach the model.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work splits into generating the query, checking it, and running it under constraints. Generation usually means prompting a model with a schema description and a user request, sometimes with examples of valid queries. Checking can be done with a parser that rejects multiple statements, comments, and unexpected keywords, with a read only database role, or with a separate model asked to classify the query as safe or not. Running under constraints means row limits, timeouts, and a role that can only touch the tables the task needs. Testing follows the same pattern as classic injection testing, with payloads placed in the fields the model reads, including documents and retrieved passages rather than only the visible input box.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership usually sits with the team that owns the data application, not with a separate AI group, because the database account and its permissions are the control that matters most. Policies tend to cover what the model is allowed to read, whether generated queries are reviewed before execution, and how prompts and retrieved documents are logged and retained. Provenance matters on both sides: where the input text came from, and which model version produced the query that ran. Review of generated SQL before it reaches production is common in regulated settings, and audit trails that tie a query back to the prompt that produced it are the usual way that review is made possible. Access reviews and credential rotation apply to the model's database account exactly as they would to any other service account.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward treating model output as untrusted input by default, with guardrails placed at the database boundary rather than only in the prompt. Expect more use of read only replicas, query allowlists, and sandboxed execution for anything a model writes. Evaluation of prompt injection resistance is becoming a routine part of testing for data applications that use language models, alongside the older injection test suites. The open questions are how to attribute a harmful query when several components contributed to it, and how to keep review practical as the volume of generated queries grows. The underlying lesson is unchanged from the early days of SQL injection: the database should never trust the string it is handed.
